name: Interdisciplinary Research
description: Interdisciplinary research in Iran connects methods and expertise across established academic fields. Documented examples include computational approaches to cognition and collaborations linking environmental science, geological hazards, and cultural history.

seo.title: Interdisciplinary Research in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore documented connections between cognition, computing, environmental management, geological hazards, and cultural research in Iran.

content.heading: Where disciplines meet
content.content:
Some research questions sit between familiar university departments. Understanding perception can require experiments with human participants alongside computational models; managing a protected landscape can require ecological evidence alongside knowledge of livelihoods. Iranian examples illustrate both approaches, although the available institutional records describe particular activities rather than the scale of interdisciplinary research across the country. [s1][s3]

A useful way to read these examples is to ask what each field contributes. Interdisciplinarity becomes tangible when researchers combine methods, data, or interpretations around a shared question. Simply bringing institutions together establishes an opportunity for collaboration; evidence of completed research requires a further step. This distinction matters especially when reading announcements of new agreements. [s1][s2]

content.heading: Cognition, experiments, and computing
content.content:
A research recruitment page from Mehdi Sanayei’s laboratory describes projects associated with the School of Cognitive Sciences at the Institute for Research in Fundamental Sciences, commonly abbreviated IPM. Its doctoral information identifies entry routes through cognitive sciences, electrical engineering, and computer engineering. The laboratory’s stated work includes psychophysics, cognitive modelling, and neural data analysis. [s1]

Psychophysics investigates relationships between physical stimuli and perception. The advertised human-participant projects concern time perception and predictive processing, while separate analysis projects use existing animal datasets to examine the thalamus in behaviour and cognition. Programming in Python or MATLAB appears alongside neuroscience knowledge among the requested skills. These are concrete examples of experimental and computational expertise meeting within a research programme. The recruitment page does not establish clinical effectiveness, national research capacity, or whether its advertised positions remain open. [s1]

content.heading: Environmental questions and cultural knowledge
content.content:
A September 2026 announcement from the UNESCO Chair on Coastal Geo-Hazards Analysis describes a memorandum linking the chair, the Research Institute for Earth Sciences at the Geological Survey of Iran, and the Natural Disasters Research Institute with its UNESCO Chair on Natural Disasters Management. Its proposed subjects extend from drought, climate, and remote sensing to geo-archaeology, past climates, and historical or literary studies concerning Persian myths. [s2]

The agreement provides for joint projects, publications, researcher exchanges, and meetings to identify priorities. Financing is to be negotiated, and particular activities may require separate agreements. It therefore documents an agreed framework and research intentions, rather than completed discoveries. [s2]

A separate UNESCO project record links evidence about natural resources and biodiversity with sustainable livelihoods at designated sites, including biosphere reserves, geoparks, and World Heritage sites. It also identifies green-economy skills and site-management capacity as intended contributions. Read together, these records show how environmental work can connect scientific evidence with management and social questions. They do not demonstrate that the intended environmental or livelihood improvements have already occurred. [s3]

content.title: What the coastal geo-hazards memorandum establishes
content.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["Coastal Geo-Hazards Chair"] -->|"Participates in"| D["Research cooperation framework"]
  B["Research Institute for Earth Sciences"] -->|"Participates in"| D
  C["Natural Disasters Institute and Chair"] -->|"Participates in"| D
  D -->|"Provides for"| E["Joint research and publications"]
  D -->|"Provides for"| F["Researcher exchanges and meetings"]
  D -->|"Leaves to further negotiation"| G["Activity financing and implementation details"]
```
content.summary: The arrows identify participation and provisions of the announced agreement. They do not represent supervisory authority, confirmed funding, or completed research outputs.

content.heading: Recognizing an achievement
content.content: These examples offer different kinds of evidence: a laboratory describes research methods and training expectations; a memorandum sets out cooperation; a project portal records intended management activities. Each helps explain how fields connect, but none alone measures national success. Assessing achievement requires matching the claim to the evidence—for example, examining published results for a scientific finding or an evaluation for an asserted practical benefit. [s1][s2][s3]

name: Education Challenges
description: Education challenges in Iran involve access, learning, institutional capacity, and the transition from study to work. Evidence also documents unequal access to digital learning and additional disruption to schooling during the 2026 emergency.

seo.title: Education Challenges in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Understand documented pressures on education access, learning, digital participation, skills development, and continuity of schooling in Iran.

content.heading: Access, learning, and continuity
content.content:
Evaluating education requires several distinct questions. Can learners enter and remain in education? Do they acquire the intended knowledge? Can they continue learning when buildings or services are disrupted? UNESCO’s education monitoring separates participation, completion, learning proficiency, resources, and teacher indicators. That structure helps explain why a single enrolment statistic cannot describe the whole system. [s1]

For Iran, the inspected evidence supports a connected account of these pressures, but with uneven coverage. UNHCR documents school-capacity constraints affecting displaced learners, while reporting on remote education identifies equipment and connectivity barriers for vulnerable Iranian and refugee households. More recent humanitarian reporting records physical disruption to education. These sources concern different populations and reporting periods; their findings should not be combined into an undated national failure rate. [s2][s3][s4]

content.heading: Resources and classroom capacity
content.content:
The annual series below reports education expenditure relative to gross domestic product, the value of economic output. This ratio provides context for the resources allocated to education, but does not show spending per learner, purchasing power, the distribution of funds, or classroom effectiveness. Its missing observations must remain visible. [s1]

Capacity pressures are more tangible in UNHCR’s reporting. Its update covering April 2025 describes overcrowded classrooms in refugee-hosting areas and attributes an estimate of additional national school-construction needs to the government. These are reported needs, rather than an independently completed census of school conditions. They nevertheless show why an entitlement to education can coexist with difficulty obtaining an available place. [s2]

content.title: Iran: government education expenditure as a share of GDP
content.interpretation: The inspected UIS profile reports a higher share in 2018 than in 2013, followed by lower reported shares in 2022 and 2023. The gap in 2021 prevents an uninterrupted annual reading. These ratios do not establish changes in real spending per student.

content.heading: Participation does not establish learning
content.content:
UNESCO reports minimum proficiency separately from participation and completion. This is a useful distinction for reading claims about education quality: attendance records show involvement in schooling, while assessments investigate particular learning outcomes. Neither should be treated as a complete measure of a child’s educational experience. The inspected country profile also contains substantial gaps, limiting what can be said about recent change. [s1]

During pandemic closures, UNHCR reported that students could in principle use Shaad, Iran’s remote-learning application, but that practical access depended on devices and connectivity. Its account explicitly identified difficulties for vulnerable refugees and Iranians. This historical evidence explains a mechanism of unequal participation: providing a platform does not establish that every household can use it. It does not measure the extent of digital exclusion in 2026. [s3]

content.heading: From education to working life
content.content:
Skills and employment form another part of the challenge. UNICEF’s announcement of the TORANJ programme describes an initiative joining education, life readiness, and employment-related skills in Kermanshah, Isfahan, Shahrood, Qom, and Qeshm. Its emphasis on local capacities indicates that interventions need to respond to particular settings. [s5]

A launch announcement establishes the programme’s stated purpose and reported operation, rather than its lasting effect on employment. Participant testimonials are also different from a representative evaluation. This distinction applies more broadly to claims that a training course, university partnership, or entrepreneurship scheme has resolved a skills mismatch. Such claims require evidence about subsequent outcomes and the people included in the assessment. [s5]

content.heading: Keeping learning possible during emergencies
content.content:
Emergency preparedness was already an education concern before the 2026 hostilities. UNICEF and the Iranian Red Crescent Society reported training volunteers in inclusive early childhood education during emergencies, including child protection, communication, disability inclusion, and psychosocial support. The activity demonstrates preparation and training, rather than proof that every affected child received uninterrupted education. [s6]

OCHA’s update covering late March and early April 2026 subsequently described school-damage assessments, closures where buildings were unsafe, and schools being used as temporary shelters. It also reported efforts to rehabilitate schools, support connectivity, and establish temporary learning provision. These conditions add safety and continuity to longer-standing access questions. The update is a dated emergency snapshot; it does not establish the condition of all schools at the October editorial cutoff. [s4]

The most useful reading of Iran’s education challenges therefore keeps resources, access, learning, and later opportunities distinct while examining their connections. It also keeps historical observations separate from current conditions. This overview remains incomplete on student migration, graduate employment, and university–industry outcomes, which require additional dedicated evidence.

name: Educational Equity
description: Educational equity concerns whether learners can participate and learn despite differences in disability, household circumstances, location, or documentation status. Evidence from Iran shows why formal access must be assessed alongside accessible materials, practical support, and available school places.

seo.title: Educational Equity in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Examine documented barriers to inclusive schooling in Iran, including disability access, learning materials, geography, and refugee documentation.

content.heading: What equitable participation requires
content.content:
A school place is only part of educational access. Learners also need to enter the building, obtain usable materials, communicate in the classroom, and receive appropriate support. UNICEF’s account of disability inclusion in Iran identifies shortcomings in accessible infrastructure and learning resources, alongside weaknesses in identification and data collection. This makes equity a question of how education is delivered as well as who is formally admitted. [s1]

Different barriers can overlap. A child with a disability in a remote community may face both accessibility difficulties and limited nearby provision. Research by Human Rights Watch and the Center for Human Rights in Iran identified particular exclusion risks for girls with disabilities and children living in rural or remote areas. These findings concern the research period of their report; they should not be presented as a new measurement of present-day prevalence. [s2]

content.heading: Disability: admission and meaningful inclusion
content.content:
The organizations’ report describes barriers associated with school-entry assessments, reluctant admissions, inaccessible facilities, and inadequate classroom support. Its evidence came from interviews and documentary research, with important sampling and access limitations. It establishes documented experiences and mechanisms of exclusion, rather than a representative national rate. [s2]

UNICEF describes work with Iranian partners on teacher capacity, disability identification and referral, assistive technologies, and better information systems. These activities address different parts of the pathway into learning: identifying support needs does not by itself make a classroom accessible, while equipment alone does not supply trained assistance. Programme intentions must therefore be distinguished from independently demonstrated changes in participation. [s1]

content.heading: Learning materials as essential infrastructure
content.content:
Braille provides a concrete example of the resources required for inclusion. In February 2025, UNICEF reported procuring a braille embosser for the Ministry of Education and Special Education Organization to improve textbook production. Its account describes older machines as unreliable and attributes difficulty procuring replacement equipment directly to international sanctions. These are UNICEF’s descriptions of the intervention and its procurement context. [s3]

The distinction between delivering a machine and improving a learner’s experience remains important. The announcement establishes procurement and the intended contribution to accessible materials. It does not independently verify that every pupil subsequently received the right textbook before classes began. Evaluating equity would also require evidence on delivery, usability, and classroom support. [s3]

content.heading: Afghan learners and changing administrative barriers
content.content:
UNHCR’s factsheet covering January–September 2024 describes foreign children studying alongside Iranian pupils, but also records constraints: registration depended on a Yekta identification code and available school capacity. Its account demonstrates why broad statements about inclusive policy need to be read alongside the administrative conditions operating in a particular school year. [s4]

A subsequent UNHCR update reports an April 2025 instruction in Tehran province prohibiting registration of students holding headcount slips for the following academic year. This was a specific reported restriction affecting a documentation category, rather than evidence that every Afghan child was excluded everywhere. The update does not establish whether that instruction was later modified or how consistently it was implemented. [s5]

Assessing educational equity therefore requires information about both rules and lived access, disaggregated by relevant circumstances. The evidence here documents important barriers and responses, but a complete national account still requires current data on household income, geography, gender, language, disability, and documentation status.
